title: Sum of Numbers
story: Legend says the mathematician Gauss, as a child, was asked to sum all numbers from 1 to 100. While his classmates added manually, Gauss spotted a pattern and solved it instantly. You'll build two functions — one that sums from 1 to n, and another that sums any range.
why: Summation functions reinforce the accumulator pattern with addition and demonstrate how parameterizing start and end values creates a more general-purpose tool.
analogy: Summing numbers is like filling a jar with coins. Each iteration drops one coin (the current i value) into the jar (total). The jar starts empty (total=0), and by the end of the loop, it holds the sum of all coins dropped. `sum_range` lets you choose which set of coins to drop — not always starting from coin 1.
try_it: Use `sum_to` to verify Gauss's shortcut: sum_to(n) should equal n × (n+1) / 2. Write a function `gauss_check(n)` that computes both methods and returns true if they match. Test with n=100, n=50, and n=1000.
tips: Start the accumulator at 0 — the additive identity (adding 0 changes nothing)
For sum_range, initialize the loop counter to `start` not 1
Handle edge cases first: n < 1 for sum_to, start > end for sum_range
sum_to(n) is equivalent to sum_range(1, n) — verify this in your code
common_mistakes: Starting total at 1 instead of 0 — adds an extra 1 to every result
Using `<` instead of `<=` in the loop — misses the last number in the range
Forgetting to handle invalid ranges (start > end) — can cause infinite loops
Confusing sum_range parameters — sum_range(10, 20) sums 10 through 20, not 10 items starting at 20
